items.title: OpenAI ships GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol — cheaper, and the first model to hit “High” on self-improvement capability
items.summary: Astra (frontier) and Sol (efficient) both beat their GPT-6 predecessors while costing less: Astra scores 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Agents' Last Exam at under a third the cost, and sets a new high on Terminal-Bench-Science (+9 points, also under a third the cost). API pricing for Astra drops 20% on input/output with a 60% cached-input discount. Astra is also the first OpenAI model to hit “High” on self-improvement capability under OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, triggering a new internal oversight process.
items.why: A flagship upgrade that's both better and meaningfully cheaper is rare — and OpenAI flagging its own model as newly capable of self-improvement is a safety signal worth knowing, not just the speed bump.
items.action: If you're on a paid plan, run one of your existing long-horizon coding prompts through Sol instead of Astra and compare cost vs. quality.

eval.reason: Genuine new flagship+efficient model pair with real benchmark and pricing changes; not a rehash of the Sept GPT-6 Astra brief.

items.title: Google extends Agent Anomaly Detection to agents on AWS, Azure, or on-prem — via telemetry only
items.summary: Previously Google-Cloud-only, Agent Anomaly Detection now reviews agents anywhere, as long as their OpenTelemetry traces/logs reach a GCP project — via Workload Identity Federation, so an agent trades its AWS role or Microsoft Entra identity for short-lived Google credentials with no service-account key involved. In two real test deployments it caught an AWS Lambda inventory agent being scraped page-by-page, and a Microsoft Foundry customer-service agent that approved a $999 refund on a $15.99 order after a prompt injection, plus a fake “store administrator” issuing $1,784.90 in unauthorized refunds.
items.why: A concrete, told-with-receipts example of prompt injection and agent misuse actually getting caught in production — exactly the kind of monitoring worth having on any agent with real permissions, wherever it runs.
items.action: If you're running an agent built with ADK for Python 2.12.0+ outside GCP, check whether your traces already meet the OpenTelemetry + resource-attribute requirements.

items.title: Simon Willison: run Claude Code, Codex or Pi against a real sandbox with two npx commands
items.summary: Three working prototype sandboxes (WebAssembly/v86, Apple Containers, Microsoft Quicksand+QEMU) all implement the same protocol, so any of Claude Code, Codex or Pi can execute commands inside one — the agent runs on your Mac as usual, but every command is confined to the folders you mount and the network hosts you explicitly proxy-allow, with API keys injected by the proxy so the agent never sees them directly.
items.why: A real, runnable answer to “what happens when my coding agent does something I didn't want” — not a policy or a prompt, an actual filesystem/network boundary you can stand up in minutes.
items.action: Worth testing against your own harness tooling — run its riskier steps through one of these sandboxes before trusting it on a less-reviewed code path.

items.title: New DeepLearning.AI course: Evaluating and Improving Agentic Applications (with Arize Phoenix)
items.summary: Taught by Laurie Voss (Arize's Head of Developer Relations, npm co-founder), built with Arize AI. Covers reading agent traces, labeling recurring failures into a reusable test set, building code-based evaluators and calibrated LLM judges (measured with precision, recall and Cohen's kappa), and verifying agent tool-calls and outcomes, not just final text.
